title: Pelican AI brings 25 years of banking AI to faster, safer global payment screening

title: Antonio Bravo (BBVA): “AI Will Help Us Build a Better, More Profitable Bank With Greater Growth Potential”
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence Updated: 11 Nov 2026. Antonio Bravo (BBVA): “AI Will Help Us Build a Better, More Profitable Bank With Greater Growth Potential”. Antonio Bravo, Global Head of AI Transformation at BBVA, spoke at two events in London organized by Bloomberg and the Financial Times, outlining the key elements of BBVA’s strategy to deploy artificial intelligence across the organization and bring its benefits to customers. After more than a year developing agents, and with AI tools now available across the organization, BBVA is moving toward a new model for scaling the technology safely and with robust governance and controls. “We are already rolling out our first AI solutions, and the pace of launches will accelerate even further next year,” Bravo said. Communications. Listen to audio Leer en español. At these specialist events in London’s financial district, BBVA explained how the transformation strategy is being driven from the top , with an impact across every business area, and how it seeks to engage employees throughout the Group, based on the conviction that AI will be essential to sustaining growth and serving customers better. “At BBVA, we believe AI can help us remove bottlenecks and bring its benefits into the day-to-day experience of our customers and employees. We want to use AI to build a better bank for our customers—one that is more profitable and has greater growth potential in the countries where we operate—creating value for our shareholders and new opportunities for our employees,” Antonio Bravo said during Bloomberg Tech Week. Those early developments are already beginning to deliver results. Together with OpenAI, with which it has a strategic partnership to develop these agents , BBVA is working in Spain and Mexico on solutions for customer service, support for relationship managers and risk analysis. Initial results show a 30% reduction in the time spent on certain tasks involved in preparing enterprise financial risk programs, while early versions of the mobile AI assistant are already handling around half of the text-based queries that previously went to relationship managers. But bringing these advances to the entire organization requires a step change in scale. As Bravo explained at the Financial Times event , BBVA has moved beyond an initial learning phase characterized by ad hoc development for individual projects, which helped the bank understand how to build AI agents, what data they need and how to connect them to its systems. BBVA creates a model to scale AI across the Group and drive its customer-centric transformation.

title: OCBC Launches AI Assistant for Business Account Maintenance
excerpt: Share LinkedIn Facebook Twitter Copy Link Telegram Email. Free Newsletter. Get the hottest Fintech Singapore News once a month in your Inbox. OCBC has launched an AI assistant called Velocity Smart Assist on its Velocity business banking platform. The bank said the tool lets business customers complete account maintenance requests digitally within minutes, as reported by Asian Banking & Finance. In its first phase, Velocity Smart Assist focuses on managing who has access to a business account. Customers can add or remove users and approvers, assign and amend user roles, identify the parties who need to approve a change and route the request digitally for review. OCBC said these are among the most common requests businesses make. According to the bank, businesses submit 20,000 account maintenance requests a year. From 2027, OCBC plans to extend the assistant to cover additional maintenance requests. These include updates to transaction authorisation limits, registered business names and mailing addresses. The bank will roll out Velocity Smart Assist progressively to business banking customers across its core markets. In Singapore, nearly 200,000 business banking customers use Velocity. OCBC is applying AI in other parts of its business. Its private banking arm, Bank of Singapore, uses agentic AI through a platform called HELIOS to cut account opening times for wealth clients to 15 business days. title: KI-Governance: Nur jede fünfte Bank hat ihre Modelle ausreichend unter Kontrolle
excerpt: Drei von vier Banken weltweit (76 Prozent) rechnen damit, dass KI bis 2031 eigenständig Entscheidungen über Kreditrisiken und andere Risikobewertungen treffen kann und wird. Doch gerade einmal 18 Prozent verfügen bislang über umfassende Governance-Prozesse für den KI-Einsatz. Das zeigt eine internationale Studie des Softwareanbieters SAS. Auch bei der Überwachung und Nachvollziehbarkeit der eingesetzten Modelle bestehen erhebliche Defizite. D ie Studie „Why AI at Scale Needs Governance at Speed“ basiert auf der Befragung von 300 Führungskräften aus Banken in 31 Ländern. Durchgeführt wurde sie von SAS gemeinsam mit FT Longitude und Microsoft. Demnach ist Künstliche Intelligenz im Bankensektor schon recht weit verbreitet: Immerhin 82 Prozent der Institute nutzen generative KI, 41 Prozent setzen auf agentenbasierte KI-Systeme (Agentic AI). Einschließlich traditioneller Verfahren wie Machine Learning verwenden praktisch alle befragten Banken KI für Kreditentscheidungen oder Risikobewertungen. Bei 59 Prozent ist die Technologie zumindest teilweise in die Entscheidungsprozesse integriert. Zu den wichtigsten Einsatzgebieten zählen die Bewertung von Kreditrisiken (63 Prozent) und das Asset and Liability Management (55 Prozent). Allerdings entwickeln sich die Kontrollmechanismen deutlich langsamer als der KI-Einsatz. Demnach verfügt gerade mal jede fünfte Bank über vollständig integrierte AI-Governance-Prozesse. Ein Viertel der Institute hat noch nicht einmal spezifische Richtlinien für das Risikomanagement seiner KI-Modelle etabliert. Besonders deutlich werden die Defizite beim laufenden Betrieb der Systeme. Lediglich 19 Prozent der befragten Banken nutzen ein Echtzeit-Monitoring, um Veränderungen und Abweichungen im Verhalten ihrer KI-Modelle zu erkennen. 42 Prozent haben keine definierten Abschaltmechanismen, sogenannte Kill Switches, mit denen sich problematische Modelle gezielt deaktivieren lassen. Nur 36 Prozent aktualisieren ihre Modelle regelmäßig oder trainieren sie neu. Bankenaufsicht warnt vor zu schneller KI-Einführung. Hinzu kommt ein Transparenzproblem: Fast zwei Drittel der Banken wären nach eigenen Angaben bereit, ein nicht erklärbares Blackbox-Modell einzusetzen, wenn dieses bessere Ergebnisse oder eine höhere finanzielle Performance verspricht als eine nachvollziehbare Alternative. Gleichzeitig berichten 92 Prozent der Befragten, dass in ihrem Unternehmen mindestens ein Large Language Model außerhalb des bestehenden Governance-Rahmens entwickelt oder eingesetzt wird. Damit entstehen Risiken für die Einhaltung regulatorischer Anforderungen, insbesondere wenn KI-Systeme unmittelbar in Kreditentscheidungen oder andere risikorelevante Prozesse eingebunden werden. Wenn KI-Systeme falsche Entscheidungen treffen, hat das ganz reale Konsequenzen für die Kunden einer Bank sowie für ihr Image und ihre Profitabilität. Schnelle KI-Einführung allein reicht nicht. Eine funktionierende Governance in Verbindung mit skalierbarer Trustworthy AI schafft erst die Resilienz, Compliance und Verantwortlichkeit, die moderne Banken für den Geschäftserfolg brauchen. “. Anselmo Marmonti, Vice President of Risk, Fraud and Compliance Solutions, SAS. Auch die europäische Bankenaufsicht sieht die Entwicklung kritisch. „Die KI-Ambitionen einer Bank dürfen nicht größer sein als ihre tatsächlichen Governance-Fähigkeiten“, erklärt Marilin Pikaro, Director of Innovation, Conduct and Consumers bei der Europäischen Bankenaufsichtsbehörde EBA. Selbst vielversprechende Anwendungsfälle dürften demnach nicht schneller vorangetrieben werden, als die Institute in der Lage seien, die damit verbundenen Risiken zu beherrschen. Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen ein grundsätzliches Problem: Während Banken zunehmend KI-gestützte und perspektivisch autonome Entscheidungen anstreben, fehlen vielerorts noch die technischen und organisatorischen Voraussetzungen, um diese Systeme zuverlässig zu überwachen, ihre Entscheidungen nachzuvollziehen und bei Fehlentwicklungen rechtzei

title: The Future of Banking: Strategy for the AI Era
excerpt: . The Future of Banking: Strategy for the AI Era. AI is reshaping banking economics, competition, and customer relationships, forcing banks to rethink where to lead, how to compete, and AI’s role. By Michael Kochan, Peter Stumbles, Roberto Frazzitta, James Hadley, and Christy de Gooyer. Table of Contents. Progress:. en. At a Glance. AI could reshape where banks make money—and what constitutes a defensible competitive advantage. Banks need to reassess where to defend leadership, rethink participation, and build new sources of distinctive value. Four questions can help executive teams pressure test their strategy and set course for an AI-led future. What can AI do for my bank?. It’s a question every bank CEO is asking today, and for good reason. Banking sector economics have been under pressure for decades (see Figure 1). Over the next five years, agentic AI may further disrupt the industry by altering which banking businesses remain structurally attractive, which competitive moats endure, and which customer relationships prove worth defending. It has the potential to lower barriers to entry, reset costs, strip friction from profitable products, and upend customer relationships. But viewing AI only through the lens of productivity and disruption misses another side of the opportunity: It can also help build genuinely superior propositions that take share with increased speed. Figure 1. Banks with No. 1 or close No. 2 positions in their business lines have measurably higher return on equity (ROE) than those with weaker leadership positions (see Figure 2). Setting the right strategy remains essential. AI may change how defensible those leadership positions are and where new ones can be built. So before asking what AI can do for the bank, leaders need to ask where and how the bank should compete in an AI-led future. Figure 2. Banks can pressure test their current strategy for an AI future by exploring a series of high-gain questions: Where can we build and defend positions that will be difficult to displace? Where should we rethink how we participate as existing positions become more exposed? And where can AI help create propositions that offer customers distinctive value?. Those choices are what should inform any bank’s AI agenda and the allocation of capital and resources behind it. Four hard truths for an AI-led future. 1. Profit pools built on inattention and inertia are the most exposed. Many traditional banking advantages—physical footprint, brand, customer primacy, trust, and product integration—work because they help keep customers in place. That has proved remarkably durable. Customers do not continually compare every deposit rate, loan, fee, or financial product available to them. Switching takes time and effort. Banks have been hearing about disruption from digital attackers for years. But even when challengers—whether upstart or incumbent rival—offered compelling products and experiences, customers still had to take action to switch. That friction has helped incumbents. AI agents could change that equation. If comparing offers, identifying better terms, or switching providers becomes dramatically easier, businesses that benefit from customers staying put could become more vulnerable. Services and tools already exist to monitor deposit rates and help move cash toward higher-yielding accounts, and to redirect payroll and recurring bills. Agents could make finding and acting on better offers easier. This could give digital attackers a better opportunity to move beyond areas where they have already made strong inroads, such as payments, into money management, simpler forms of lending, and potentially, over time, other parts of the banking relationship. title: Atomic targets capital raise to fuel agentic AI work
summary: CEO and co-founder Jordan Wright said the fintech seeks to raise between $30 million and $50 million, although AI firms capturing investor attention has made the fundraising climate more challenging.
excerpt: An article from. Atomic targets capital raise to fuel agentic AI work. CEO and co-founder Jordan Wright said the fintech seeks to raise between $30 million and $50 million, although AI firms capturing investor attention has made the fundraising climate more challenging. Published Nov. 11, 2026. Caitlin Mullen Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. Fintech Atomic FI is working to raise capital in the coming months as it seeks to expand its services to help banks meet the artificial intelligence agent moment. Salt Lake City-based Atomic is targeting an equity capital raise of between $30 million and $50 million, CEO and co-founder Jordan Wright said during an interview at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. Founded in 2019, Atomic has focused on direct deposit and payment switching and subscription management. The fintech works with nine of the top-10 banks and counts about 350 clients, Wright said. Wright said he expects current and new investors to participate in the funding round. Capital One Ventures, Citi Ventures and FNB Corp. all took part in the company’s April 2025 $10 million strategic fundraise , which brought Atomic’s total to about $79 million. Wright indicated the fintech is eyeing more strategic investments from large banks it works with. “I could see a world where we take in some strategic money and ask our current investors to back off a little bit, so that we can get some more strategic money around the table,” he said. The artificial intelligence frenzy has affected the fundraising climate, Wright noted. He referenced investors that, a year ago, would have been eager to participate in Atomic’s fundraise that are now entranced by AI companies and their growth potential. “The dynamic has been, with those companies, a little bit challenging, but then there's been a whole series of investors that are like, ‘Hey, we still like companies with good unit economics, good fundamentals, great clientele,’ which we have,” he said. Atomic declined to share revenue figures, but a spokesperson said the firm doubled its revenue from 2025 to 2026 and expects to double it again next year. The spokesperson declined to comment on whether the company is profitable. As the onset of personal AI agents acting on consumers’ behalf alters the competitor landscape for Atomic’s bank clients, the fintech sees opportunity, said Wright and Andrea Martone, Atomic’s co-founder and chief product officer. Banks seek deterministic models and mechanisms, which operate based on code that tells them explicitly how to take an action, Wright and Martone said. Atomic has built that. The fintech is also working with Sierra AI on personal AI agent protocols. Atomic is “working on combining all the actions and data-pulling that we’ve done over time,” to build a combined platform bank and fintech clients can use to say, “‘I’m going to go compete with Muse and allow my customer to go act on the web on my behalf,’” Wright said. Last month, Fifth Third CEO Tim Spence said the bank aims to “take every valuable service that you can get done on Muse, whether that’s looking at subscriptions and finding opportunities to generate savings or budgeting or otherwise,” and build those into its app. Wright said Atomic aims to work with Cincinnati-based Fifth Third on that endeavor, since the bank is already a client of the fintech’s. The targeted fundraise will accelerate some of Atomic’s agentic work, Wright said. “We have to continue moving fast all the time, staying up to speed with what is needed,” he said. Wright sees Atomic’s existing ties to big banks and fintechs, who are “constantly directing us,” as its competitive moat. “We get pushed that direction naturally,” he said. Banks working with Atomic, in turn, get peer comparisons, since they know who the fintech’s other customers are, Martone said. title: Business Leaders Ponder AI at 25th Banking and Finance Symposium
excerpt: Business Leaders Ponder AI at 25th Banking and Finance Symposium. Annual event drew 400 attendees and raised more than $300K. Home. News. Business Leaders Ponder AI at 25th Banking and Finance Symposium. OXFORD, Miss. – The University of Mississippi's 25th Banking and Finance Symposium broke records for support and attendance as industry leaders gathered to discuss issues including cybersecurity, fraud and artificial intelligence. While technology was a theme, speakers stressed the importance of relationships and that trust and human judgment remain irreplaceable. Chancellor Glenn Boyce told attendees in his keynote address that nurturing trust is a critical factor, whether one works for a financial institution or in higher education. "The first time they lose trust in you, I'm sorry, you don't get a second time," he said. "You just don't get a second time. That's how important it is. ". Boyce identified critical thinking as one of the most important skills students must retain, even as the university incorporates AI into its courses. The goal is to teach students not to become overly reliant on technology to provide answers or to simply change the parameters until we get something we like, he said. "We can't lose our creativity and our ability to make decisions," Boyce said. "That can't be the way we move forward in the future. Even though there are people who will tell you that is the only way we are going to move forward in the future, I see it as a threat to mankind. ". One of the university's greatest strengths is that it prepares students with human skills that technology cannot replace, said Rich Gentry, dean of the School of Business Administration. "I think one of the things that differentiates the University of Mississippi from many other institutions is the focus here on relationships," he said. "At the university, we need to pair that with some technical skills, some job training, so at the business school a big focus for us going forward is going to be to some degree where we can lean into those social skills. ". AI has moved swiftly from the discussion phase to implementation in the banking industry in just 24 months, said Stan Viner, president of the school's banking and finance board. This demonstrates how important it is for students to learn how to use and coexist with AI. "To me one of the nice things about AI is that it will allow for the automation of repeatable processes, to free up the people in the bank to think more about strategic priorities," he said. Phil Buffington, one of the event's organizers and an attorney at Balch & Bingham LLP who works with banks, said he could see AI also being involved in risk assessment, regulatory guidance and cybersecurity. But businesses should use AI to assist and supplement human decision-making, not replace them, he said. "You still have to have experienced people that understand the data, that know how to read it and not only decide which way to move, but also if something is presented that does not quite add up, to be knowledgeable enough to go back and adjust it," Buffington said. "It will help banks operate with greater speed and efficiency to make an impact on the communities they serve. ". The quality of the symposium's speakers, including a "fireside chat" with Michelle "Miki" Bowman, vice chair for supervision for the Federal Reserve System's board of governors, and educational panels on technology and regulation is what keeps attendees coming back, said Chuck Nicholson, a 1981 alumnus of the school and former chairman of Community Bank. "A lot of the meetings that I go to, if I show up and it is just a social event, I don't go back," he said. BoU Calls for Safeguards as AI, Open Banking Reshape Finance
excerpt: The Bank of Uganda has called for stronger safeguards in the adoption of artificial intelligence, Open Banking and other emerging financial technologies, warning that innovation must not expose consumers to privacy violations, unfair treatment and financial instability. Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba said technological developments were creating opportunities to reduce the cost of financial services, improve delivery and extend access to underserved communities, but stressed that these benefits must be accompanied by adequate consumer protection. He said artificial intelligence could strengthen fraud detection and service provision, while Open Banking and Open Finance could allow customers to benefit from the secure sharing of their financial information. However, Nuwagaba warned that customers must understand how their personal financial data are collected and used, while also having avenues to challenge decisions affecting them. “Privacy, security, fairness and accountability must be considered from the outset,” he said. He made the remarks on Thursday while addressing the Annual Financial Inclusion and Financial Literacy Forum 2026 at Four Points by Sheraton in Kampala. Nuwagaba also called for careful examination of the implications of virtual assets, stablecoins and tokenisation on consumers, financial integrity and financial stability. He said technological innovation should not leave behind people without smartphones, reliable internet connectivity, digital skills or acceptable identification documents. The Deputy Governor challenged financial institutions, fintech companies, telecommunications operators and regulators to work together to ensure that emerging financial products are affordable, accessible and trustworthy. He said financial literacy should also evolve to equip consumers with the knowledge to navigate increasingly complex digital financial services and protect themselves against fraud. Nuwagaba further emphasised the responsibility of financial service providers to explain charges and contractual terms clearly and establish accessible mechanisms for handling customer complaints. Beyond the technology agenda, he said Uganda needed a financial system capable of supporting productive sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, mineral development and information and communication technology. He said inclusive financing could help mobilise savings, reduce transaction costs and enable businesses to invest, expand and create employment in support of the government’s Ten-Fold Growth Strategy. Meanwhile, Nuwagaba said the Bank of Uganda was strengthening its regional role in financial inclusion policy and coordination. He said the central bank had been elected Vice-Chair of the African Financial Inclusion Policy Initiative (AfPI) for a two-year term in July 2026 in Angola and would host the initiative’s conference in Uganda in 2029. The bank is also scheduled to host the East African Community Monetary Affairs Committee Technical Working Group meeting on financial inclusion, innovation and consumer protection. Nuwagaba said the forum should produce three to five practical commitments, with responsible institutions, implementation milestones and follow-up arrangements under the existing National Financial Inclusion Strategy II coordination framework. UK banks 'cut AI exposure' as correction fears grow, says PRA chief
excerpt: UK banks 'cut AI exposure' as correction fears grow, says PRA chief. By Dalvinder Kular 12/11/2026. UK banks have started reducing their exposure to AI-related businesses as concerns mount over a potential market correction, according to an interview with Katharine Braddick published by Bloomberg. The chief executive of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) told the newswire that banks are reassessing their appetite for AI-related risk, although the regulator has not found evidence that the sector would amplify any shock. "We're all alarmed at the moment, aren't we?" Braddick told Bloomberg, adding that while the Bank of England is not considering using capital requirements to encourage banks to reduce AI exposure, firms are reviewing their lending and investment decisions. "Banks are all asking themselves that question" of whether to reduce exposure, she said. "I can see firms looking at their risk appetite and thinking and considering, 'Yes this client, not that client. ' You do see it feed through," Bloomberg reported. According to Bloomberg, the PRA has carried out extensive assessments of banks' exposure to AI, but has not concluded that lenders would act as an "amplifier" if the sector experienced a sharp downturn. Braddick told the newswire that AI-related risks have become a "constant conversation" since she took over the regulator, alongside wider concerns around operational resilience. Last month, the PRA announced it would publish a five-year plan focusing on four priorities that Braddick believes will be central to the regulator's success: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency. Later this month the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) plan to publish guidance later this month covering risks associated with frontier AI and quantum computing. Braddick told Bloomberg the guidance would be "quite concrete", outlining governance expectations and supporting closer collaboration between regulators and the financial services industry. The PRA is also considering how to implement the Bank of England's proposed "minimum viable bank" framework, first outlined by governor Andrew Bailey earlier this year. According to Bloomberg, the framework would require banks to maintain core operational capabilities capable of delivering essential services during a cyber attack. "It's an urgent question," Braddick told Bloomberg, referring to discussions about which firms should operate their own infrastructure and how smaller banks could access shared services. She added that no timetable has been set for introducing any new requirements. Braddick said strengthening operational resilience would improve the UK's competitiveness, telling Bloomberg: "Operational resilience doesn't deliver financial resilience. But the two are out of kilter, so we need to uplift operational resilience. " Braddick was appointed as the deputy governor for prudential regulation at the Bank of England and chief executive of the PRA in March, stepping into the role in July. She took over from Sam Woods who had been in post since 2016. Prior to joining the PRA, Braddick worked as Barclays’s group head of strategic policy and senior adviser to the chief executive.
